0.title: First Steps in Following Jesus
0.essay:
If you have recently put your trust in Jesus Christ, welcome to the family of God. This is the most important decision you will ever make, and it is the beginning of a new life.

Your questions

You probably have many questions. What exactly happened to me? How can I be sure I am saved? How do I pray? Where do I start reading the Bible? Do I need to go to church? What about baptism? How do I deal with sin? This short study answers those questions simply. It is written for new Christians, but it may also help anyone who wants to be sure of the basics. Each chapter points to other studies in this app where you can go deeper when you are ready.

A relationship, not a list of rules

Jesus said, “I came that they may have life and have it abundantly” (John 10:10). The Christian life is not a list of rules but a relationship with God through Jesus, by the Holy Spirit. It begins with grace, continues by grace and ends in glory.

The chapters

What Happened When You Believed; Sure of Your Salvation; Prayer and the Bible; You Belong: Church and Baptism; and Living the New Life.

1.title: What Happened When You Believed
1.essay:
When you trusted in Jesus, several wonderful things happened, all at once, whether you felt them or not.

You were forgiven

Every sin you have ever committed, past, present and future, was paid for by Jesus on the cross. “In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace” (Ephesians 1:7). God no longer counts your sins against you.

You were made right with God

God declared you righteous, not because of anything you did, but because of what Jesus did. “Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1). Peace with God, access to God and hope in God now belong to you, as they belong to every believer.

You were born again

God gave you new life by his Spirit. “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come” (2 Corinthians 5:17). You are not just a better version of your old self; you are a new person. That does not mean you will never struggle again. It means God has begun a new work in you, and he will complete it.

You became God’s child

“But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12). This new birth does not come from human effort or family background, but from God. He is now your Father, and you belong to his family.

The Holy Spirit came to live in you

God’s Spirit lives in every believer (Romans 8:9). He helps you understand the Bible, pray, fight sin and grow.

It was all grace

“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9). You did not earn any of this. God gave it freely, because he loves you. And Paul goes on: “we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Ephesians 2:10). We are not saved by good works, but we are saved for them.

Turning and trusting

Becoming a Christian involves turning from sin, which the Bible calls repentance, and trusting in Jesus, which it calls faith. They go together like two sides of a coin, and both continue for the rest of your life.

Some people feel great joy when they become Christians; others feel very little. Your salvation does not depend on your feelings but on what God has done and promised.

Two stories

A jailer in Philippi, terrified after an earthquake, asked Paul and Silas, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” They answered, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household” (Acts 16:30–31). That same night he was baptised, and he “rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God” (Acts 16:34).

A young man becomes a Christian after a church course. He does not feel very different at first, and worries that it did not work. An older Christian shows him 2 Corinthians 5:17 and John 1:12: these things are true because God says so, not because he feels them. Over the following months he notices real changes in his desires and habits.

When you are ready to go deeper, the studies on the Grace of God and the Person and Work of Christ explain these truths more fully.

For reflection

Which of these things that happened when you believed means most to you, and why? Why does it matter that salvation is a gift? How would you explain to a friend, in your own words, what it means to become a Christian? Take a moment to thank God for what he did for you.

2.title: Sure of Your Salvation
2.essay:
Many new Christians wonder whether they are really saved, especially when they sin again or do not feel close to God. God wants you to be sure.

God wants you to know

“I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13). John did not write so that you would hope or guess, but so that you would know. Assurance is not arrogance; it is taking God at his word.

Based on God’s promise

Your assurance rests on what God has said. “And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. Whoever has the Son has life” (1 John 5:11–12). If you have trusted in Jesus, you have the Son, and you have life.

Held by Jesus

Jesus said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:27–28). And he added that no one can snatch them out of the Father’s hand either (John 10:29). Your security does not depend on how tightly you hold Jesus, but on how tightly he holds you.

God finishes what he starts

“And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). God does not start projects and abandon them. Your salvation is his work from beginning to end, and he will finish it. Nothing can stop him: “neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39).

When you sin

You will still sin. When you do, you are not lost. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). “But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1). Failure is not final for the believer.

Peter denied Jesus three times — the worst failure of his life. Yet Jesus had prayed for him, and after the resurrection Jesus restored him (Luke 22:32; John 21:15–19). Peter’s salvation did not depend on his performance but on Christ’s faithfulness.

A new Christian loses her temper badly with her sister and wonders whether she was ever really saved. She reads 1 John 1:9 and 2:1, confesses her sin to God and apologises to her sister. She learns that the Christian life is not about never falling, but about always coming back.

Signs of new life

Assurance rests on God’s promises, but John also describes signs of new life: believing in Jesus, loving other Christians, wanting to obey God and turning from sin. These signs grow over time, and they strengthen assurance.

True believers keep trusting Christ to the end, not because they are strong, but because God keeps them. Those who walk away for good show that they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). If you are worried about this, the worry itself is often a sign of real faith.

So ask yourself: on what do you base your assurance — your feelings, your performance or God’s promise? The Assurance of Salvation study explains all this more fully.

For reflection

Why does God want you to be sure of your salvation? What is the difference between assurance based on feelings and assurance based on God’s promises? What should you do when you sin? Try to memorise John 10:27–28 or 1 John 5:13 this week.

3.title: Prayer and the Bible
3.essay:
Every relationship grows through communication. In prayer, you speak to God. In the Bible, God speaks to you.

Prayer

Prayer is simply talking to God as your Father. You do not need special words. Jesus taught that prayer should be sincere, not for show and not full of empty phrases, because “your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matthew 6:8). Then he gave a pattern: “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:9–13). It covers praise, God’s purposes, our needs, forgiveness and protection, and it is a model for all our prayers.

Pray about everything. “Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6). Nothing is too big or too small to bring to him.

We pray to the Father, through Jesus, by the Holy Spirit. Praying in Jesus’ name (John 14:13) means coming to God on the basis of what Jesus has done, not our own goodness.

The Bible

The Bible is God’s word to you. “All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16). Paul reminded Timothy that the Scriptures “are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 3:15). They are God’s own word, given for our growth.

“Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105). It does not always show the whole road ahead, but it shows the next step. And it is food for your soul: “Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up into salvation” (1 Peter 2:2). If you have tasted that the Lord is good, you will want more.

Where to start

A good place to begin is one of the Gospels, such as Mark or John, to get to know Jesus. Then read Acts, and some of the shorter letters like Philippians or 1 John. Read the Psalms to help you pray. Read a little each day, perhaps a chapter, and ask: What does this show me about God? About Jesus? About myself? What should I believe or do?

Some parts of the Bible are hard to understand. That is normal. Ask questions, use a good study Bible or the commentaries in this app, and talk with mature Christians.

A daily habit

Try to set aside a regular time each day, even fifteen minutes, to read the Bible and pray. Many find the morning best. Jesus himself made time: “And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed” (Mark 1:35). If Jesus needed time alone with the Father, so do we. It is not a duty to earn God’s favour, but a time to enjoy him.

A new Christian who has never read the Bible starts reading Mark’s Gospel, one chapter each morning, and writes down one thing he learns about Jesus each day. After sixteen days he has finished his first book of the Bible and knows Jesus far better.

So: when and where will you read the Bible and pray tomorrow? The studies on Prayer, Spiritual Disciplines and the Big Story of the Bible will help you grow here.

For reflection

What does the Lord’s Prayer teach you about how to pray? Which book of the Bible will you start reading this week? When is the best time in your day to read and pray? Pray through the Lord’s Prayer slowly, putting each line into your own words.

4.title: You Belong: Church and Baptism
4.essay:
When you became a Christian, you joined a family. God never intended his children to live alone.

The church

The church is not a building but God’s people. “Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it” (1 Corinthians 12:27). Paul says the church is like a body with many parts, and every part matters: “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of you’” (1 Corinthians 12:21). You have a place in Christ’s body, and the body needs you. You need other Christians, and they need you.

So do not go it alone. “And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another” (Hebrews 10:24–25). Christians who stay away from church usually struggle to grow. God has chosen to work through his church — through preaching, baptism, the Lord’s Supper, fellowship and the care of elders. These are often called the means of grace.

Finding a good church

Look for a church where the Bible is faithfully taught, Jesus is at the centre, the gospel is clear and people genuinely care for one another. Go regularly. Get to know people. Ask about membership.

A woman who came to faith through an online video is nervous about going to church. A friend offers to go with her. She finds a warm welcome, joins a small group and is baptised a few months later. She says that belonging to the church has helped her grow more than anything else.

Baptism

Jesus commanded his followers to be baptised (Matthew 28:19). Baptism is a public sign that you belong to Jesus. It pictures your sins washed away and your union with Christ in his death and resurrection: “We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). Every time you remember your baptism, you remember that your old life died with Christ and your new life belongs to him.

Baptism does not save you, but it is an important step of obedience. In the New Testament people were baptised soon after believing. On the day of Pentecost Peter called the crowd to repent and be baptised, and “those who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls. And they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers” (Acts 2:41–42). Belief, baptism and belonging went together from the start.

Christians differ over whether infants should be baptised. The New Testament examples show baptism following a profession of faith, and that is the practice this study follows; the studies on the Church and Covenant Theology explain the question more fully. If you have not been baptised as a believer, speak to a pastor about it.

The Lord’s Supper

Jesus also gave his church a meal to remember him: bread and wine, representing his body and blood (1 Corinthians 11:23–26). Baptised believers share in it regularly, remembering his death and being strengthened by him.

Serving

Every Christian has gifts to serve others in the church (1 Peter 4:10). Look for ways to help, however small. The Church and Worship and the Lord’s Day studies cover all of this in more detail.

Have you found a church family? If not, what is your next step?

For reflection

Why do you need other Christians, and why do they need you? What should you look for in a church? Have you been baptised as a believer? If not, what is your next step? How could you begin serving in your church?

5.title: Living the New Life
5.essay:
“Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving” (Colossians 2:6–7). You began by trusting Jesus; you continue the same way.

Keep walking

Paul gives three pictures in those verses: rooted like a tree, built up like a building, established in the faith — and overflowing with thanks. The Christian life continues as it began, by trusting Jesus.

Fighting sin

You will still face temptation and sin. That is normal. But now you have the Holy Spirit to help you. “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh” (Galatians 5:16). The flesh and the Spirit are at war, but the Spirit grows fruit in you: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Some habits may change quickly; others will take time. Do not give up. When you fall, confess and get up again. Growing involves effort — reading, praying, resisting sin — but it is God who gives the growth: “for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

Changed priorities

“I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship” (Romans 12:1). Every part of your life now belongs to God: your time, money, relationships, work and body.

Telling others

You have the best news in the world, and you do not need to be an expert to share it. When Jesus healed a man possessed by demons, the man begged to go with him. Jesus said, “Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you” (Mark 5:19). The man told people throughout the Decapolis, the region of ten cities, and everyone marvelled. Like the blind man Jesus healed, you can simply say, “One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see” (John 9:25). Be ready to explain your hope, gently and respectfully (1 Peter 3:15).

A new Christian tells her best friend what has happened to her. The friend is sceptical, but over the next year notices how much she has changed: calmer, kinder, more honest. Eventually the friend asks to come to church with her. Who is one person you could tell about what Jesus has done for you?

Facing hardship

Becoming a Christian does not mean life will be easy. Some new believers face opposition from family or friends, and Jesus warned that following him would be costly. But he also promised, “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

Growing

The Christian life is a journey, and you will not become mature overnight. Peter’s last words were, “But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity” (2 Peter 3:18). Growth is lifelong, and its goal is Christ’s glory. Keep reading, praying, belonging and obeying, and God will grow you.

It is wise to find an older, mature Christian of the same sex to meet with, pray with and ask questions. And when you are ready, the Fighting Sin, Evangelism and Christian Suffering studies will help you as you grow.

For reflection

What does it mean to “walk in” Christ as you received him? Which sin or habit do you most need the Spirit’s help to overcome? Who could you tell about what Jesus has done for you? What is one step you can take this week to grow in your faith?
